title: Event Sourcing Fundamentals
description: Learn what event sourcing is, how it differs from CRUD, and why you might choose it for your system.

data.text: Most applications store the current state of data. If you update a customer's address, the old address is overwritten. Event sourcing takes a different approach: instead of storing the current state, you store every change that has ever occurred as a sequence of immutable events. The current state is derived by replaying all events from the beginning.

In an event-sourced system, every state change produces an event. An event is a factual record of something that happened, such as `OrderPlaced`, `PaymentReceived`, or `ShipmentDispatched`. Events are append-only and never modified or deleted. To reconstruct the current state of an entity, you read all events for that entity and apply them in order.

data.caption: How event sourcing captures and replays state changes
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant API
    participant EventStore
    participant ReadModel
    User->>API: Update Order Status
    API->>API: Validate command
    API->>EventStore: Append OrderShipped event
    EventStore-->>API: Event persisted
    API->>ReadModel: Notify projection
    ReadModel->>ReadModel: Update materialized view
    ReadModel-->>User: Return updated state

data.text: Traditional CRUD systems overwrite state. If a bug causes bad data to be written, the original value is lost unless you have a separate audit log. Event sourcing preserves every change as a first-class citizen. You can answer questions like 'What was the order total three months ago?' or 'Who changed the shipping address and when?' without any additional auditing infrastructure.

terms.definition: An immutable record of something that happened in the past.
A cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit for data changes.
A read model built by consuming events and updating a query-optimized view.
A specialized database optimized for appending and reading ordered event streams.

data.title: Defining an OrderShipped Event
data.content: Events are simple data classes that describe what happened. They should be immutable and serializable.

data.title: Good Fit
items: Financial systems requiring a complete audit trail
Systems where historical state queries are important
Complex domains with clear temporal business rules
Event-driven microservices needing a shared source of truth
Systems requiring temporal queries (state at a point in time)

data.title: Not Every System Needs Event Sourcing
data.text: Event sourcing adds complexity. Simple CRUD applications with no audit or temporal requirements are often better served by a traditional database. Choose event sourcing because your domain genuinely benefits from it, not because it sounds interesting.

items.question: Does event sourcing mean I cannot use a relational database?
items.answer: Not at all. You can store events in a relational database using an append-only table with a sequential ID. Specialized event stores like EventStoreDB are optimized for this pattern, but a well-designed SQL table can work for simpler use cases.

items.question: What happens if an event is wrong?
items.answer: Because events are immutable, you do not edit them. Instead, you append a compensating event, such as OrderShipmentCorrected, that fixes the downstream effects. This preserves the complete history while still correcting the current state.
